title: LLD in Python: LRU cache, rate limiter, parking lot
seriesDescription: Python and FastAPI interview topics in JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short Python/SQL code and multi-correct questions. Python only: nothing here mixes in Java.
description: Low-level design in Python: an LRU cache on OrderedDict, a thread-safe token bucket class, a parking lot with abstract base classes, design patterns and thread-safety follow-ups.
source: Python docs (collections.OrderedDict, abc, functools, threading); Head First Design Patterns; Grokking the OOD interview problem lists; LeetCode 146 discussion

questions.prompt: Write a Python class LRUCache with __init__(self, cap), get(key) returning -1 on a miss, and put(key, value), using collections.OrderedDict so both operations are O(1).

checks.label: moves a used key to the end

questions.explanation: OrderedDict is itself a hash map plus a doubly linked list. The functools.lru_cache decorator is the standard-library answer when you only need function memoisation.

questions.prompt: Write a thread-safe Python class TokenBucket(capacity, refill_per_second) with a try_acquire() method that returns True or False, refills lazily from elapsed time (never above capacity), starts full and takes one token on success.

checks.label: caps tokens at capacity with min()

questions.model:
import threading, time
class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, capacity, refill_per_second):
        self.cap, self.rate = capacity, refill_per_second
        self.tokens, self.last = capacity, time.monotonic()
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
    def try_acquire(self):
        with self.lock:
            now = time.monotonic()
            self.tokens = min(self.cap, self.tokens + (now - self.last) * self.rate)
            self.last = now
            if self.tokens >= 1:
                self.tokens -= 1
                return True
            return False
questions.explanation: Lazy refill avoids a timer thread. Use time.monotonic rather than wall-clock time, which can jump. The lock makes the read-refill-decrement sequence atomic. Other correct versions use asyncio.Lock for async code.

questions.prompt: Write Python for a parking lot: an abstract base class Vehicle with an abstract method spots_needed(self), and a concrete class Car(Vehicle) that needs 1 spot.
questions.explanation: Instantiating Vehicle raises TypeError, and subclasses that forget the method also cannot be instantiated. An enum.Enum for VehicleType is the usual companion.

questions.prompt: An LRU cache has capacity 3. Operations: put(1), put(2), put(3), get(1), put(4), get(3), put(5). What is the sum of the keys left in the cache?
questions.explanation: After put(4) key 2 is evicted; after get(3) the order is 1,4,3 (oldest first); put(5) evicts 1. Remaining keys 4, 3, 5 sum to 12.

questions.prompt: A token bucket has capacity 5 and refills 2 tokens per second. It starts full, 5 requests are accepted at t = 0, then 10 requests arrive at t = 1.5 s (all at the same instant). How many of those 10 are accepted?
questions.explanation: 1.5 s x 2 tokens/s = 3 tokens were refilled, so 3 requests succeed and 7 are rejected.

questions.prompt: Match each parking-lot or cache design need to the pattern that fits best.

left.text: Switch between hourly and flat pricing or LRU and LFU eviction
Create the right Spot subclass from a type
Update display boards when a spot is taken
A ticket moves from ISSUED to PAID to EXITED

questions.explanation: Name the pattern only after stating the problem it solves. Strategy is the most frequent LLD answer (pricing, eviction, rate-limiting algorithm).

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: An LRU cache built from a hash map and a doubly linked list supports O(1) get and put.
questions.reason: The map finds a node directly and the doubly linked list can unlink and move it without scanning.

whys.a: Right: lookup is O(1) via the map and reordering is O(1) via the list pointers.

questions.explanation: A singly linked list would need the previous node to unlink, forcing an O(n) search.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: Define PricingPolicy as an interface so the parking lot can swap pricing rules.
questions.reason: Python abstract base classes refuse instantiation while abstract methods are missing.

whys.a: The ABC behaviour does not explain why an interface helps swapping.
whys.b: Right: both true, but swapping comes from programming to an interface, not from ABC enforcement.

questions.explanation: Inject the policy through the constructor so tests can pass a fake.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: OrderedDict with move_to_end is a convenient base for an LRU cache.
questions.reason: OrderedDict makes the whole get-then-reorder sequence atomic, so concurrent callers never need a lock.

whys.a: The reason is false, so it cannot explain the assertion.
whys.b: The reason is false, not merely unrelated.
whys.c: Right: single operations are safe but the check, reorder and read in get() are separate steps, so a lock is still needed.
whys.d: The assertion is the true statement.

questions.explanation: Guard get and put with one threading.Lock. For production, a library cache with locking built in is the usual answer.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: The Spot class should compute the parking fee for the vehicle it holds.
questions.reason: The Single Responsibility Principle says a class should have one reason to change.

whys.d: Right: pricing changes for business reasons unrelated to spots, so the assertion is false while the reason is true.

questions.explanation: Put pricing in a PricingPolicy used by the Ticket or a payment service.

questions.text: An OrderedDict reorders a used key with {1}, evicts the oldest entry with popitem(last={2}), and an ordinary dict keeps {3} order.
questions.explanation: move_to_end(key) sends a key to the most recent end; popitem(last=False) removes from the least recent end. Plain dicts also keep insertion order since 3.7, but have no move_to_end.

questions.prompt: Why is an OrderedDict LRU unsafe for concurrent readers even if the threads only call get?

options.text: get() reads then reorders, so another thread can evict in between
options.why: Right: the key may disappear between the membership check and the move, raising KeyError or corrupting the order.

options.text: OrderedDict raises RuntimeError whenever two threads read at the same time
options.why: No such rule exists; reads from several threads are allowed.

options.text: OrderedDict objects are bound to the thread that created them
options.why: Objects are not thread-bound; any thread can use a shared reference.

options.text: move_to_end copies the whole mapping, so concurrent reads see stale data
options.why: move_to_end relinks one node and copies nothing.

questions.explanation: Use a lock around get and put, or a cache library with locking built in.

questions.prompt: Which are sound LLD practices for the parking lot? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use an Enum for VehicleType rather than free strings
options.why: Right: it is exhaustive and typos fail early.

options.text: Inject the pricing and allocation strategies through constructors
Return an explicit Optional[Spot] (None when full) from find_spot
options.why: Right: the absence case is part of the signature.

options.text: Give the constructor a mutable default such as spots=[]
options.why: That list is created once and shared by every lot, which causes hidden coupling.

questions.explanation: Clarify requirements, list entities, define interfaces, then write the core flow park and unpark first.

questions.prompt: In Python, a class with an @abstractmethod that does not inherit from ABC (or use ABCMeta) still cannot be instantiated.

options.why: The decorator alone has no effect without the ABCMeta metaclass.
Right: abstract enforcement needs ABCMeta (usually via inheriting ABC); the decorator by itself is only a marker.

questions.explanation: Running a class with @abstractmethod but no ABC base shows A() still instantiates fine.

questions.prompt: True or false: decorating an instance method with functools.lru_cache keeps references to the instances, so they can stay alive as long as the cache does.

options.why: Right: the instance is part of every cache key, so the cache holds a strong reference to it.
Incorrect: the cache stores self in its keys, so it prevents the instance from being garbage collected.

questions.explanation: Cache a module-level function instead, or build a per-instance cache in the constructor, when instances are short-lived.
